papers.why_read: Olah's short case for treating a trained network as a compiled program to be decompiled: parameters as binary, activations as memory, and interpretable features as the variables without which reverse engineering cannot start.
papers.reading_focus: The program–network analogy table, the curse-of-dimensionality argument for reading weights rather than input–output behaviour, why activations must be split into independently understandable variables, privileged bases, and the FAQ on what a feature is.
papers.in_context: The founding statement of the reverse-engineering programme: later choices of basis — neurons, dictionaries (46), rotations (23), parameter components (66) — all answer its demand for interpretable variables. 03 still calls decomposition the central unsolved step, 02 traces how Olah's term drifted, and 85 tests the reverse-engineering analogy on a real chip.

papers.curriculum_title: Mechanistic?
papers.verified_title: Mechanistic?
papers.authors: Naomi Saphra; Sarah Wiegreffe
papers.redistribution_note: Not Creative Commons licensed: copyright remains with the authors; included as published.
papers.why_read: A short history and sociology of the word ‘mechanistic’: four competing senses of the term, and how a safety-motivated community arriving from vision research and online forums came to repeat much of NLP interpretability under a new label.
papers.reading_focus: The four definitions (narrow and broad, technical and cultural), Olah's coinage as a break from saliency methods, the parallel histories of probing, attention maps and neuron analysis, the clash of communities, and the closing appeal to connect.
papers.in_context: Read it before the canon it describes. It traces the term to a break with saliency maps, the methods 84 cast doubt on, and argues the newer community went on to repeat the probing debates of 30 and 31, placing 12 in that older tradition. 03 cites it on the term's ambiguity; its conclusion points to the safety-side scepticism of 87.

papers.why_read: Defines the Transformer — multi-head attention, residual blocks, positional encodings — the architecture every later paper reverse-engineers.
papers.reading_focus: Scaled dot-product and multi-head attention, Q/K/V projections, residual + LayerNorm structure, positional encodings, and the attention visualizations in the appendix.
papers.in_context: The architecture the rest of the collection takes apart. 01 casts it as the virtual machine on which learned programs run, 10 rewrites its attention layers as sums of paths, and 12 relies on its residual connections to read predictions mid-network. 02 recalls that NLP researchers were already probing it before the mechanistic community turned to language.

papers.why_read: The working manual for seeing what a vision neuron responds to by optimising the input, and an early, frank admission that neurons may not be the right units: one GoogLeNet neuron answers to cats, foxes and cars.
papers.reading_focus: Optimisation objectives, why optimisation separates causes from correlates, diversity terms, neuron interaction and random directions, the high-frequency ‘enemy’, the regularisation spectrum, and decorrelated Fourier preconditioning.
papers.in_context: The main instrument of 07, 08 and 09. It weighs its own experience against 06, which found basis directions more interpretable than random ones, and its cat-fox-car neuron anticipates the polysemanticity 33 formalises. It sets attribution aside; 84 shows how gradient explanations of that kind can fail basic sanity checks.

papers.why_read: Turns unit interpretability into a number: each CNN unit's activation map is scored against densely labelled concepts, showing that interpretability is tied to the basis and is destroyed by rotation without loss of accuracy.
papers.reading_focus: The Broden dataset and IoU scoring, the random-rotation experiment, unique detectors per layer, comparisons across architectures and supervised or self-supervised tasks, and the training-condition ablations (dropout, batch normalisation).
papers.in_context: The quantitative counterpart to the qualitative tools of 05 and 07, and early evidence that the neuron basis is privileged — the idea 01 builds on and 10 and 35 examine in transformers. Its fixed vocabulary of human concepts is the limit 39 later lifts with free-text labels; its first author went on to co-write 18.

papers.why_read: A deliberately exhaustive study of one neuron family in InceptionV1, written to persuade sceptics that meaningful features exist: curve detectors examined through feature visualisation, dataset labelling, attribution and synthetic stimuli.
papers.reading_focus: The four claims (causality, generality, purity, family), the hand-labelled comparison of over 800 images, joint and radial tuning curves, synthetic curves and angles, the curve families across layers, and the unexplained combing effect.
papers.in_context: The worked example behind 07's first claim, built with 05. Its purity claim — no meaningful secondary function — is the neuron-level position that 33 and the dictionaries of 45–49 gave up for language models; its first author defends it again in 64. Compare its many-method validation with the single scores of 06 and 39.

papers.why_read: Shows that networks trained on modular addition do not reliably rediscover one algorithm: small changes to hyperparameters and initialisation yield the known Clock, a new Pizza algorithm, or several imperfect copies running in parallel.
papers.reading_focus: Why gradient symmetricity and logit patterns rule out the Clock, the Pizza algorithm and circle isolation, accompanying pizzas, the distance-irrelevance metric, and the phase diagram over attention rate and width.

papers.curriculum_title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT

papers.why_read: Uses causal tracing — corrupting the subject, then restoring single hidden states — to locate factual recall in the mid-layer MLPs of GPT models, then rewrites individual facts there with a rank-one weight edit (ROME).
papers.reading_focus: The causal-tracing heatmaps and their early and late sites, the MLP-severing experiment, the MLP-as-associative-memory derivation behind ROME, the CounterFact specificity–generalization results, and the stated limitations.
papers.in_context: The claim in this section's first pair: localization shows where a fact is stored, and so where to edit it. 19 tests that inference and finds it fails; 24 proposes a mechanism for the gap. Its associative-memory view of MLPs revises the per-neuron reading of 36, its Gaussian-noise corruption is one of the choices 26 compares, and 29 studies self-repair on its CounterFact prompts.
